# Economic cost-effectiveness {#sec-economic}

The concept of economic cost-effectiveness, developed by the PRC, is defined as the sum of gate-to-gate ATM/CNS provision costs and en‐route and airport ground ATFM delays costs, expressed per composite flight-hour. This economic performance indicator is intended to capture trade‐offs between these two components, with delays arising from temporary imbalances between available capacity and traffic demand[^3].

[^3]: See <https://ansperformance.eu/economics/ace/ace-handbook/> for more information on the methodology used to compute composite flight-hours and economic costs.

@fig-figure-3-1 shows [preliminary results]{.underline} on the changes in economic cost-effectiveness over {{< var doc.year_report_minus10 >}} - {{< var doc.year_report >}} at Pan-European system level. Unit economic costs fell by -7.1% in 2025, driven by a -18.8% decrease in the unit costs of ATFM delays, and a -2.8% reduction in ATM/CNS provision costs per composite flight-hour. Although gate-to-gate ATFM delays fell from 29.6 million minutes in 2024 to 25.2 million minutes in 2025, they remained relatively high, with estimated costs of €3.4 billion. ATFM delay costs accounted for 23% of unit economic costs, down from the record high of 27% in 2024 but close to the shares recorded in 2018, 2019 and 2023.

For ten ANSPs ATFM delays represented more than 30% of their unit economic costs (see ANSPs with the largest red and yellow portions, e.g. M-NAV, BHANSA, HASP, SMATSA, DSNA, etc.). In absolute terms (cumulative ATFM delays in minutes) DSNA, ENAIRE and HASP generated 50% of the Pan-European system total ATFM delays.

The primary sources of ATFM delays in 2025 were capacity and staffing shortages (47% of total ATFM delays), followed by adverse weather conditions (34% of total ATFM delays). 

Further analysis of the relationship between changes in ANSPs costs, traffic and unit costs will be presented in the forthcoming ACE report.
